data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The preference for corroborated theories inevitably smuggles induction back into Popper's system, rendering his rejection of probabilistic confirmation inconsistent with scientific practice, because any rational preference for action logically entails an expectation of future success which can only be grounded in the inductive assumption that past performance predicts future results.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If 'preference' can be decoupled from 'expectation of success' and redefined purely as a procedural rule.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the cost of abandoning induction is shown to be the abandonment of rational action itself.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If Popper's system allows for 'blind' preference where the agent admits they have no reason to expect success but chooses anyway.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Analyzes the logical structure of 'rational preference.' Argues that to prefer X over Y for the purpose of achieving a goal Z implies a belief that X is more likely to achieve Z than Y. Since Popper denies that corroboration increases probability, the only remaining basis for this belief is an implicit inductive principle: that the properties which allowed X to survive past tests will persist. Thus, the 'pragmatic' defense is a disguised form of induction.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
